title: Homily II — Into your hands, my Son

edition.locus: Migne, PG 96 (Paris, 1860), Homily II on the Dormition, col. 736 (PDF leaf 409)

source_text: Εἶτα τούτοις συνῳδὰ καὶ ἀκόλουθά τινα δοκεῖ πεπρᾶχθαι τὸ τηνικάδε, ὥς μοι δοκεῖ. Ἡ τοῦ βασιλέως πρὸς τὴν οἰκείαν λοχεύτριαν ἔλευσις, χερσὶ θείαις καὶ ἀκηράτοις ὑποδεξομένου τὴν ἱερὰν ταύτης ψυχὴν, καὶ εἰλικρινῆ τε καὶ ἄμωμον. Καὶ αὕτη μὲν οἷα εἰκὸς ἔφησεν· « Εἰς χεῖράς σου, τέκνον ἐμὸν, τὸ πνεῦμά μου παρατίθημι. Δέξαι μου τὴν σοὶ φίλην ψυχὴν, ἣν ἐτήρησας ἄμεμπτον. Σοὶ τὸ ἐμὸν σῶμα, καὶ οὐ τῇ γῇ παραδίδωμι. Φύλαξον σῶον, ὃ κατοικῆσαι ηὐδόκησας, καὶ γεννηθεὶς Παρθένον ἐτήρησας. Πρὸς ἐμὲ μετάστησον, ἵν' ὅπου εἶ σὺ, τῶν ἐμῶν σπλάγχνων τὸ κύημα, ἔσομαι κἀγὼ σοὶ συνέστιος. Πρός σε γὰρ ἐπείγομαι τὸν πρὸς ἐμὲ ἀδιαστάτως καταφοιτήσαντα. Σὺ τοῖς ἐμοὶ ποθεινοτάτοις τέκνοις, οὓς ἀδελφοὺς καλέσαι ηὐδόκησας, τῆς ἐμῆς ἐκδημίας γενοῦ παραμύθιον. Πρόσθες εὐλογίαν ἐπὶ τὴν εὐλογίαν αὐτῶν διὰ τῆς τῶν ἡμῶν χειρῶν ἐπιθέσεως. » Εἶτα τὰς χεῖρας ἐπάρασα, οἷα εἰκὸς, τοὺς συνειλεγμένους εὐλόγησε, τοιαῦτα προσομιλήσασα τὰ ῥήματα, καὶ· « Δεῦρο, ἡ εὐλογημένη μου Μήτηρ, εἰς τὴν ἀνάπαυσίν μου, ἀκούσασα. Ἀνάστα, ἐλθὲ, ἡ πλησίον μου, ἡ καλὴ ἐν γυναιξὶν, ὅτι ἰδοὺ ὁ χειμὼν παρῆλθεν, ὁ καιρὸς τῆς τομῆς ἔφθασε. Καλὴ ἡ πλησίον μου, καὶ μῶμος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν σοί. Ὀσμὴ μύρων σου ὑπὲρ πάντα τὰ ἀρώματα. » Τούτων ἡ ἁγία ἀκούσασα, τὸ πνεῦμα ταῖς χερσὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ παρατίθεται.
pass_a_gloss: Then things concordant (συνῳδά) and consequent with these seem (δοκεῖ) to have been done (πράσσω) at that time, as it seems to me. The coming (ἔλευσις) of the King to his own (οἰκεία) child-bearer, [he] about to receive with divine (θεῖος) and undefiled hands her holy (ἱερός) soul (ψυχή), both pure and blameless (ἄμωμος). And she, as is likely, said: 'Into your hands (χείρ), my child, I commit my spirit (πνεῦμα). Receive (δέχομαι) my soul dear (φίλη) to you, which you kept (τηρέω) unblameable. To you my body (σῶμα) and not to the earth (γῆ) I hand over. Guard (φυλάσσω) safe (σῶος) what you were well pleased (εὐδοκέω) to dwell in, and, having been born, kept a Virgin (Παρθένος). Remove [me] to yourself, so that where you are, the conceived one (κύημα) of my inward parts/womb (σπλάγχνα), I too shall be your hearth-sharer/housemate. For to you I hasten, who came down to me without separation/interval. You, to my most longed-for children (τέκνα), whom you were pleased to call brothers (ἀδελφοί), become the consolation of my departure (ἐκδημία). Add blessing (εὐλογία) upon their blessing through the laying-on (ἐπίθεσις) of [printed: our, τῶν ἡμῶν] hands.' Then lifting up (ἐπαίρω) her hands, as is likely, she blessed (εὐλογέω) those gathered (συλλέγω), having addressed such words (ῥήματα), and having heard (ἀκούω): 'Come (δεῦρο), my blessed Mother (Μήτηρ), into my rest. Arise (ἀνίστημι), come, my near one, the fair (καλή) among women; for behold the winter (χειμών) has passed, the time (καιρός) of pruning (τομή) has arrived (φθάνω). Fair [is] my near one, and blemish (μῶμος) there is not in you. Smell (ὀσμή) of your ointments (μύρα) above all the spices (ἀρώματα).' Having heard these, the holy one (ἡ ἁγία) commits her spirit to the hands of the Son (Υἱός).
pass_b_english: Then, as it seems to me, things were done at that hour in keeping with these words and following on from them. The King comes to her who gave him birth, to receive in his divine and undefiled hands her holy soul, pure and spotless. And she, as one may suppose, said: "Into your hands, my child, I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46; Psalm 31:5). Receive my soul, which is dear to you and which you kept blameless. To you, and not to the earth, I hand over my body. Keep safe the body you were pleased to dwell in, you who at your birth kept me a virgin. Take me to yourself, so that where you are, you whom my womb conceived, I too may be, sharing your home (John 14:3). For I hasten to you, who came down to me without any separation. Be yourself the comfort of my departure to my dearest children, whom you were pleased to call brothers (Hebrews 2:11). Add blessing upon their blessing through the laying-on of my hands."

Then, raising her hands, as one may suppose, she blessed those who were gathered there, having spoken to them such words as these. And she heard: "Come, my blessed Mother, into my rest. Arise, come, my dear one, fair among women (Song of Songs 1:8); for see, the winter is past, the time of pruning has come (Song of Songs 2:10-12). You are fair, my dear one, and there is no blemish in you (Song of Songs 4:7). The fragrance of your perfumes is beyond all spices (Song of Songs 4:10)." Hearing these words, the holy one commits her spirit into the hands of her Son.

choices.note: I commit my spirit" is Christ's word from the cross (Luke 23:46), itself from Psalm 30:6 LXX = Psalm 31:5 (English numbering), with "my child" in place of "Father".
The printed margin gives Song of Songs 2:10-11; the clause "the time of pruning has come" (ὁ καιρὸς τῆς τομῆς ἔφθασε) is Song 2:12 LXX, so the citation is given as 2:10-12.
"Fair among women" (ἡ καλὴ ἐν γυναιξίν) is inserted from Song 1:8 LXX (also 5:9; 6:1).
ἡ πλησίον μου (the Song's term of endearment, literally "my near one") rendered "my dear one".

The print's quotation marks enclose both "Come, my blessed Mother, into my rest" and the Song verses, with the participle ἀκούσασα ("having heard") set inside them; the Song words are taken as continuing the Son's call, as the closing "Hearing these words" shows.
"Come ... into my rest" may echo Psalm 132:8 (LXX 131:8, "Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark") or Matthew 25:34; uncertain, left uncited.
Printed διὰ τῆς τῶν ἡμῶν χειρῶν ἐπιθέσεως ("of our hands") is rendered "my hands": Mary is the speaker and the sense expects τῶν ἐμῶν; the oddity is the print's.
λοχεύτρια (usually "midwife" or "woman in childbirth") here means she who bore him; rendered "her who gave him birth".

ἀδιαστάτως ("without interval or separation") rendered literally "without any separation"; it probably means that the Word came down without being parted from the Father, but that is not spelled out and is not added.
οἷα εἰκός ("as is likely") marks the author's reconstruction, rendered "as one may suppose".
Παρθένον ἐτήρησας: the relative clause shifts from the body to Mary herself ("kept [me] a virgin");
The section's opening ἔλευσις sentence has no finite verb; rendered with "comes".

Printed Πρὸς ἐμὲ μετάστησον (literally "move to me") is confirmed on the page image (col. 736, leaf 409); it is rendered by its evident sense, "take me to yourself", which the PG Latin also gives ("Transfer me ad te").
The printed τῶν ἡμῶν χειρῶν is likewise confirmed on the image; the PG Latin has "manuum mearum".

variants.printed: διὰ τῆς τῶν ἡμῶν χειρῶν ἐπιθέσεως ('our hands')
variants.basis: Mary is the speaker; PG Latin 'manuum mearum'; print confirmed on leaf 409
